lessons.title: Correlation Regimes and Their Impact on Risk Parity

children.text: Every risk parity calculation in this course so far has treated correlation as a fixed input: minus 0.10 between equity and debt, 0.05 between equity and gold, 0.00 between debt and gold. Real correlations are not fixed. They cluster into regimes, hold for months or years, and then shift, sometimes gradually and sometimes overnight. This lesson asks the question a risk manager cannot avoid asking: what happens to a risk parity portfolio built on yesterday's correlations when tomorrow's correlations are different.

markDefs.definition: A macroeconomic environment during which the correlation between two or more asset classes stays relatively stable, before shifting to a different stable relationship in a different environment.

children.text: is the macro backdrop that determines whether equity and debt help or hurt each other. In a disinflationary growth regime, the one this course has assumed throughout, weak growth data pushes central banks toward rate cuts, which lifts bond prices right as equity sells off on the same weak data. That is the mechanism behind the mildly negative equity-debt correlation used in every case study so far. In an inflation-shock regime, the relationship flips: a central bank raising rates to fight inflation hurts bond prices through higher yields at the very same time high rates and inflation fears hurt equity valuations. Both fall together.

India lived through exactly this second regime in 2022. The RBI raised the repo rate from 4.00% in April 2022 to 6.50% by February 2023 to fight inflation running above its target band. Over roughly the same stretch, Nifty 50 corrected from its October 2021 peak while G-Sec prices fell as yields rose in lockstep with the repo rate. Equity and debt were not offsetting each other that year, they were both responding to the same inflation and rate shock in the same direction.
The Crisis Correlation Problem: When Diversification Disappears Exactly When You Need It

There is a second, sharper version of this problem, sometimes summarized as 'correlations go to 1 in a crash.' During an acute liquidity panic, leveraged participants across the market face margin calls simultaneously and sell whatever can be sold to raise cash, not just the asset that started the panic. In the first two to three weeks of the March 2020 crash, even gold, normally the portfolio's steadiest diversifier, sold off alongside Nifty 50 as funds and traders liquidated positions across every asset class to meet margin calls. Gold only decoupled and began behaving like a safe haven again once the immediate liquidity panic eased and central banks, including the RBI, stepped in with rate cuts and liquidity support.

body.text: This is the cruelest version of the correlation problem. A risk parity portfolio is built specifically to survive drawdowns better than a concentrated equity book, by spreading risk across sleeves that are not supposed to fall together. In the acute phase of a genuine liquidity crisis, that exact assumption can fail for days or weeks, right when the portfolio needs it most.

children.text: Take the same three-asset portfolio from chapter 2, still with equity, debt, and gold volatility held fixed at 14%, 5%, and 12%, and compare the familiar normal-regime correlations against an illustrative stress-regime set where an inflation shock and a liquidity scramble hit at once: equity-debt correlation flips from -0.10 to +0.40, equity-gold rises from 0.05 to +0.30, and debt-gold rises from 0.00 to +0.10.

children.text: Take the 20.12% / 57.65% / 22.24% weights this course solved for under normal-regime correlations, and, without changing them at all, recompute portfolio volatility and risk contribution using the stress-regime correlation matrix instead. This answers the question a risk desk actually cares about: how does my existing, already-placed portfolio behave if the regime shifts under it.

body.title: Risk contribution drift when correlations shift, weights unchanged (illustrative)

body.text: Two things happen at once, and both matter. First, total portfolio volatility jumps by about 26%, from 4.74% to roughly 5.99%, purely because correlations converged, not because any single asset's own volatility changed. Second, the risk balance itself breaks down: equity's share of total risk overshoots its 33.3% target by more than four percentage points, gold's undershoots by about five, even though nobody touched the weights. The portfolio quietly became an equity-tilted, gold-light risk profile exactly during the regime where that tilt is least wanted.

children.text: Now look at the last column: the weights you would get if you had somehow known the stress regime was coming and solved for equal risk contribution under it directly. They are not dramatically different, equity trimmed from 20.1% to 18.4%, gold raised from 22.2% to 24.6%. And critically, portfolio volatility barely improves, 5.97% versus 5.99%. Rebalancing to the new regime restores equal risk contribution, but it does almost nothing to undo the rise in total portfolio risk. That rise comes from the diversification benefit itself shrinking when correlations converge, and no amount of reweighting three assets can fully manufacture diversification that the market has stopped offering.
What Practitioners Actually Do About This
Nobody has solved correlation regime shifts. What real risk parity desks do is manage the exposure to the problem, not eliminate it.

body.title: Three Practical Responses to Correlation Regime Risk

columns.label: Faster-reacting correlation estimates
points: Use exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) correlation instead of a flat trailing window, so recent data is weighted more heavily
Shortens the lag between a regime actually shifting and the portfolio's correlation estimate catching up
Trade-off from chapter 2's lesson on lookback windows still applies: faster reaction means more noise

columns.label: Routine correlation stress testing
points: Run the exact calculation from this lesson regularly, not once at portfolio construction: apply a stress correlation matrix to current weights and check how far risk contribution drifts
Turns regime risk from a blind spot into a monitored, quantified exposure
Does not prevent the drift, but makes it visible before it shows up as an unexplained drawdown

columns.label: Adding a genuine diversifier
points: Some institutional risk parity funds add a trend-following or managed-futures sleeve specifically because it tends to perform differently in exactly the regimes where equity and bonds fall together
Adds complexity and its own estimation challenges
A structural answer rather than a monitoring answer, addressed only briefly here as it is a large topic in its own right

body.code:
import numpy as np

def rc_shares(weights, cov):
    weights = np.array(weights)
    port_vol = np.sqrt(weights @ cov @ weights)
    mctr = (cov @ weights) / port_vol
    rc = weights * mctr
    return port_vol, rc / port_vol

def correlation_stress_test(weights, vol, corr_normal, corr_stress):
    cov_normal = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr_normal
    cov_stress = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr_stress
    pv_n, rc_n = rc_shares(weights, cov_normal)
    pv_s, rc_s = rc_shares(weights, cov_stress)
    return {
        'normal_vol': pv_n, 'normal_rc_share': rc_n,
        'stress_vol': pv_s, 'stress_rc_share': rc_s,
    }

weights = np.array([0.2012, 0.5765, 0.2224])
vol = np.array([0.14, 0.05, 0.12])
corr_normal = np.array([[1, -0.10, 0.05], [-0.10, 1, 0.00], [0.05, 0.00, 1]])
corr_stress = np.array([[1, 0.40, 0.30], [0.40, 1, 0.10], [0.30, 0.10, 1]])

result = correlation_stress_test(weights, vol, corr_normal, corr_stress)
print('Normal regime: vol =', f"{result['normal_vol']:.2%}", ' rc% =', np.round(result['normal_rc_share']*100, 1))
print('Stress regime: vol =', f"{result['stress_vol']:.2%}", ' rc% =', np.round(result['stress_rc_share']*100, 1))
body.caption: Run this against your own current portfolio weights and a range of plausible stress correlation matrices, not just one. The output tells you exactly how far your risk balance would drift if the regime shifted tomorrow, before it actually happens.

body.title: Reporting to the Risk Committee
body.scenario: You run the correlation stress test above on your desk's live risk parity portfolio and get the same pattern as this lesson's case study: portfolio volatility would rise about 26% and equity's risk contribution would overshoot its target by roughly 4 percentage points if correlations shifted to the stress regime. The risk committee asks what action this finding requires today.
body.prompt: What would you actually recommend, given that re-solving ERC weights under the stress regime barely reduced the volatility increase in this lesson's case study?
body.modelAnswer: Since reweighting alone did almost nothing to reduce the volatility increase (5.97% versus 5.99% in the case study), the honest recommendation is not 'quietly rebalance to fix it,' because that would not meaningfully fix it. The more useful actions are process-level: flag the exposure explicitly so the committee understands current risk estimates assume a regime that may not hold, tighten monitoring so a real shift is caught quickly rather than discovered after a drawdown, and separately evaluate whether a structural diversifier, such as a trend-following sleeve, is worth adding given the desk's mandate and risk appetite. Reweighting the existing three sleeves is not the lever that solves this problem.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In the case study, why did re-solving ERC weights under the stress-regime correlations barely reduce portfolio volatility, even though it did restore exactly equal risk contribution?
options: Because the solver failed to converge under the stress correlations
Because equal risk contribution only redistributes a fixed amount of total risk across assets, it does not create diversification benefit that correlation convergence has already destroyed
Because gold's volatility rose sharply in the stress scenario
Because the stress correlations used were too small to matter
body.explanation: Reweighting can rebalance which asset is responsible for how much risk, but the total amount of risk in the portfolio is driven by how much the assets move together. When correlations converge upward across the board, the underlying diversification benefit shrinks, and no redistribution of weights across the same three assets can fully restore risk that correlation convergence has removed.

body.text: Risk parity's equal risk contribution property holds exactly for whichever correlations you solved it with, and drifts the moment those correlations change. Correlation regime shifts, whether the slow kind driven by an inflation cycle or the sudden kind driven by a liquidity crisis, do two things at once: they unbalance the portfolio's risk shares, which reweighting can fix, and they shrink the underlying diversification benefit, which reweighting mostly cannot fix. Managing this risk means monitoring it continuously, not solving it once at construction.

points: Correlation regimes shift between disinflationary growth periods, where equity and debt offset each other, and inflation-shock periods, like India's 2022 rate-hiking cycle, where they fall together.

In acute liquidity crises, such as the first weeks of March 2020, correlations across nearly all risk assets can converge toward 1 as leveraged participants sell everything to meet margin calls, even assets like gold that normally diversify equity risk.

In this lesson's illustrative case study, shifting from normal to stress-regime correlations, with weights unchanged, raised portfolio volatility by about 26% and pushed equity's risk contribution roughly 4 percentage points above target while gold's fell roughly 5 points below.

Re-solving ERC weights under the stress regime restored exact equal risk contribution but barely reduced the volatility increase, because reweighting cannot manufacture diversification benefit that correlation convergence has already removed.

Practical responses include faster-reacting correlation estimates (such as EWMA), routine correlation stress testing of the kind performed in this lesson, and, for some institutional portfolios, adding a structurally different diversifier such as a trend-following sleeve.
The next lesson moves to Hierarchical Risk Parity, a machine-learning-inspired approach that changes how the correlation structure itself is used, rather than assuming it is stable.
